extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review, journal editors, publishers, funders, and policy-makers interested in scholarly publishing and peer review studies
extracted.subtask_description: A multidisciplinary review identifying gaps in theoretical and empirical understanding of journal-coupled and alternative peer review systems, and providing a roadmap and research priorities for a new field of Peer Review Studies. The paper highlights measurable dimensions, methodological needs, and policy recommendations for editors, reviewers, publishers and funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of editors and editorial decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a non-uniform and heterogeneous set of roles across journals, typically focused around decision-making processes; editorial peer review has become more of a judicial role (binary accept/reject) than a critical examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how editorial roles vary by journal and discipline; study whether journals send all submissions to peer review or selectively desk-reject; examine editorial comments versus reviewer comments; investigate how editors signal which reviewer comments are important. Consider collecting data on number of rejections prior to acceptance and acceptance rates to understand editorial behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of editorial criteria and justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifications or criteria for editorial rejections and decisions are rarely given or automated and are poorly known, causing frustration for authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should provide transparent justifications for decisions (e.g. handling editor identity, scope/fit reasons, editorial comments). Sharing such information would improve legitimacy and enable study of editorial standards; beware that disclosure could lead to status-based superficial judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial conflicts of interest and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often fail to disclose their conflicts of interest, which can compromise objectivity and influence decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and study disclosure of editors' other professional roles, interactions with authors/reviewers, and potential COIs. Investigate how commercial/publisher interests might conflict with editorial independence and how disclosure affects perceptions of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer impartiality and sources of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer impartiality is affected by author nationality, institutional prestige, reviewer nationality, gender, discipline, confirmation bias, publication bias and many personal factors (workload, psychography, emotional state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure systematic biases at scale and system-level (not just single-journal studies). Investigate hidden social dimensions (relationships between authors and reviewers) and how journal policies relate to actual practice. Account for both subtle and large influences on reviewers' partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'peer' and reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: What defines a 'peer' and what constitutes expertise are multi-dimensional, varying across disciplines, career stage and research history, and these prescriptions are often concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify and operationalize criteria for reviewer expertise per discipline; study whether reviewers improve with experience and how expertise relates to review quality and task expectations (e.g. method/statistics review vs. narrative critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles, expectations and compliance of reviewers (including COPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations for reviewers (what tasks they should perform) vary and are largely unknown; compliance with ethical guidelines such as COPE’s 'Ethical Guidelines for peer reviewers' is not well understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must make explicit reviewer roles and expectations (e.g. recommendation vs. detailed methodological checking). Collect data on policy compliance (e.g. fraction of reviewers who sign reports during blinded review) and whether reviewers meet role expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding versus open identities (open peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether blinding protects reviewers or whether openness increases accountability; evidence is mixed and context-dependent (discipline, career stage, cultural norms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically evaluate impacts of open identities on review honesty, quality, length, turn-around, decline rates and risks to early career researchers. Consider that blinding is sometimes unsuccessful and that revealing identities may expose relationships and biases but could improve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and openness of review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing review reports is proposed to increase transparency, but may deter reviewers or change tone; publicised reports will be skewed toward published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study whether making reports public changes reviewer acceptance rates, candor, length and quality, and how selection bias (only reports for published articles) affects conclusions. Compare signed vs unsigned and open vs closed reports via controlled trials where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality and measurement of peer review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no consensus on what peer review is for, what differentiates a good from a bad review, or how to define review 'quality'; quality can include methodological rigor, error detection, speed, strength of argumentation and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop operational definitions and measurable indicators of review quality (distinguish 'value' vs 'quality'); build and validate tools, checklists and instruments to assess the substantive contributions of reviews across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized peer review process metrics (empirical indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of empirical data points could be gathered to understand peer review functionality, including duration of phases, number of referee reports, length of reports, number of review rounds, availability and inspection of code/data/materials, reviewer decline rates, relative acceptance rates, decisions about openness of identity/reports, desk rejection proportions, ultimate manuscript fate, and whether editors select reviewers to generate a desired outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and share these metrics across journals/publishers to enable comparative and longitudinal studies. Use these indicators to quantify 'value add' of peer review, cost/time impacts, and to compare practices between journals, disciplines and publisher types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and reproducibility (of review and of research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions exist about whether peer review itself is reproducible (e.g. inter-reviewer reliability) and whether peer review ensures research reproducibility, since reviewers rarely reproduce experiments and often trust reported methods and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure inter-reviewer reliability, use specialist reviewers for methods/statistics, and explore automated services for checking analyses. Consider making reproducibility checks a more formal part of review and evaluate feasibility and trade-offs (time, cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and epistemic impacts of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review shapes scientific discourse, distributes academic capital, may foster epistemic homogeneity, and could suppress innovation via conservatism; its post-publication impacts and relationship to other evaluation mechanisms (e.g. journal impact factors) are poorly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study bi-directional learning effects (authors/editors/reviewers), measure how peer review influences subsequent research agendas, and assess trade-offs between innovation and quality control. Distinguish biases intrinsic to review from broader socio-cultural factors entrained into the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beyond traditional review: post-publication, decoupled and participatory platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel services decouple peer review from journals (post-publication review, preprint commenting), often with low engagement; questions remain about editorial control, quality assurance, automation, and detection of conflicts of interest in these models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate uptake, community engagement, the role of editorial oversight in open participatory models, and how quality control and reviewer selection should operate outside traditional journal workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of reviewer workload and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small pool of researchers performs the majority of reviewing work, raising concerns about reviewer fatigue, selection of 'good' reviewers, and unequal burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate reviewer recruitment practices, fatigue effects, and evaluate incentives (credits, discounts) offered by journals for reviewing. Measure how incentives influence reviewer thoroughness and willingness to perform replication-style checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation, software tools and their impact on peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Software exists to assist reviewer selection (e.g. reviewer locators) and automated checks (e.g. statistical checks), but their role and effects on who is invited and how reviews are conducted remain largely unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how automation affects reviewer diversity, invitation frequency, potential biases introduced by algorithmic selection, and the potential for automated reproducibility or integrity checks to complement human review. Monitor unintended consequences of automating parts of editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for consensus minimal standards and shared data infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing knowledge gaps requires a consensus on a minimal set of standards for what constitutes peer review and the development of a shared data infrastructure to support empirical study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders and publishers should support a coordinated programme, adopting minimal standards for metadata and data-sharing (workflow logs, review reports, decisions) to enable reproducible research into peer review practices. Guard against file-drawer problems where publishers only release favorable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, support, checklists and measurement tools for improving peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardised peer review 'check-lists', training for editors/reviewers, and R&D for tools to measure review quality are in relative infancy and concentrated in some disciplines (e.g. biomedicine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and evaluate checklists, reviewer training programmes and validation studies of assessment tools (e.g. RUBRIQ, tools cited in literature). Use shared data to refine guidance and assess effectiveness of interventions.
